title: Pragmatic clinical trial
wikitext:
{{Short description|Clinical trial that focuses on outcome correlations rather than causality}}

A '''pragmatic clinical trial''' ('''PCT'''), sometimes called a '''practical clinical trial''' ('''PCT'''),<ref name="pmid_14506122">{{Citation |last1=Tunis |first1=SR |last2=Stryer |first2=DB |last3=Clancy |first3=CM |year=2003 |title=Practical clinical trials: increasing the value of clinical research for decision making in clinical and health policy |journal=JAMA |volume=290 |issue=12 |pages=1624–1632 |pmid=14506122 |doi=10.1001/jama.290.12.1624 |postscript=.|doi-access=free }}</ref> is a [[clinical trial]] that focuses on [[correlation and dependence|correlation]] between [[therapy|treatments]] and [[outcomes research|outcomes]] in [[Real world evidence|real-world]] [[health system]] practice rather than focusing on proving [[causality|causative]] explanations for outcomes, which requires extensive de[[confounding]] with [[inclusion and exclusion criteria]] so strict that they risk rendering the trial results irrelevant to much of real-world practice.<ref name="pmid_20831305">{{Citation |last1=Mullins |first1=CD |last2=Whicher |first2=D |last3=Reese |first3=ES |last4=Tunis |first4=S |display-authors=etal |year=2010 |title=Generating evidence for comparative effectiveness research using more pragmatic randomized controlled trials |journal=Pharmacoeconomics |volume=28 |issue=10 |pages=969–976 |pmid=20831305 |doi=10.2165/11536160-000000000-00000 |s2cid=33592391 |postscript=.}}</ref><ref name="pmid_4860352">{{Citation |last1=Schwartz |first1=D |last2=Lellouch |first2=J |display-authors=etal |year=1967 |title=Explanatory and pragmatic attitudes in therapeutical trials |journal=J Chronic Dis |volume=20 |issue=8 |pages=637–648 |doi=10.1016/0021-9681(67)90041-0 |pmid=4860352 |postscript=.}}</ref>

== Examples ==
A typical example is that an [[anti-diabetic medication]] in the real world will often be used in people with (latent or apparent) [[diabetic nephropathy|diabetes-induced kidney problems]], but if a study of its [[efficacy]] and [[adverse drug reaction|safety]] excluded some subsets of people with kidney problems (to escape confounding), the study's results may not reflect well what will actually happen in broad practice. PCTs thus contrast with explanatory clinical trials,<ref name="pmid_4860352"/> which focus more on causation through deconfounding. The pragmatic versus explanatory distinction is a [[spectrum]] or [[continuum (measurement)|continuum]] rather than a [[dichotomy]] (each study can fall toward one end or the other),<ref name="pmid_19348971">{{Citation |last=Thorpe |first=KE |display-authors=etal |year=2009 |title=A pragmatic-explanatory continuum indicator summary (PRECIS): a tool to help trial designers |journal=J Clin Epidemiol |volume=62 |issue=5 |pages=464–475 |pmid=19348971 |doi=10.1016/j.jclinepi.2008.12.011 |postscript=.|pmc=2679824 }}</ref> but the distinction is nonetheless important to [[evidence-based medicine]] (EBM) because physicians have found that [[average treatment effect|treatment effects]] in explanatory clinical trials do not always translate to outcomes in typical practice. [[Decision-making|Decision-makers]] (including individual [[physician]]s deciding what to do next for a particular [[patient]], developers of [[medical guideline|clinical guidelines]], and [[health policy]] directors) hope to build a better evidence base to inform decisions by encouraging more PCTs to be conducted.<ref name="pmid_14506122"/>

== Distinction from other forms of trials ==
The distinction between pragmatic and explanatory trials is not the same as the distinction between [[randomized experiment|randomized]] and nonrandomized trials. Any trial can be either randomized or nonrandomized and have any degree of pragmatic and explanatory power, depending on its [[clinical study design|study design]], with randomization being preferable if practicably available. However, most [[randomized controlled trial]]s (RCTs) to date have leaned toward the explanatory side of the pragmatic-explanatory spectrum, largely because of the value traditionally placed on proving causation by deconfounding as part of proving efficacy, but sometimes also because "attempts to minimize cost and maximize efficiency have led to smaller sample sizes".<ref name="pmid_20831305"/> The movement toward supporting '''pragmatic randomized controlled trials''' (pRCTs) hopes to make sure that money spent on RCTs is well spent by providing information that actually matters to real-world outcomes,<ref name="pmid_20831305"/> regardless of conclusively tying causation to particular variables. This is the [[pragmatism|pragmatic]] element of such designs. Thus pRCTs are important to [[comparative effectiveness research]],<ref name="pmid_20831305"/> and {{Anchor|Efficacy versus effectiveness}} a distinction is often (although not always) made between [[efficacy]] and [[effectiveness]], whereby efficacy implies causation provided by deconfounding other variables (we know with certainty that drug X treats disease Y by mechanism of action Z) but effectiveness implies correlation with outcomes regardless of presence of other variables (we know with certainty that people in a situation similar to X who take drug A tend to have slightly better outcomes than those who take drug B, and even if we think we may suspect why, the causation is not as important).<ref name="NYT-20201120">{{cite news |last=Zimmer |first=Carl |authorlink=Carl Zimmer |title=2 Companies Say Their Vaccines Are 95% Effective. What Does That Mean? You might assume that 95 out of every 100 people vaccinated will be protected from Covid-19. But that's not how the math works. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/11/20/health/covid-vaccine-95-effective.html |date=20 November 2020 |work=The New York Times |accessdate=21 November 2020 }}</ref>

Explanation remains important, as does traditional efficacy research, because we still value knowledge of causation to advance our understanding of [[molecular biology]] and to maintain our ability to differentiate real efficacy from [[placebo|placebo effect]]s. What has become apparent in the era of advanced [[health technology]] is that we also need to know about comparative effectiveness in real-world [[applied science|applications]] so that we can ensure the best use of our limited resources as we make countless instances of clinical decisions. And it is apparent that explanatory evidence, such as [[in vitro]] evidence and even [[in vivo]] evidence from clinical trials with tight exclusion criteria, often does not help enough, by itself, with that task.<ref name="pmid_20831305"/>

==Other types of pragmatic research==
[[Pragmatism]] can be used as an [[epistemology]] when undertaking any type of research.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yvonne Feilzer|first=Martina|date=2010-01-01|title=Doing Mixed Methods Research Pragmatically: Implications for the Rediscovery of Pragmatism as a Research Paradigm|journal=Journal of Mixed Methods Research|language=en|volume=4|issue=1|pages=6–16|doi=10.1177/1558689809349691|s2cid=220267495 |issn=1558-6898}}</ref> Examples include systematic reviews, consensus methods such as [[Delphi method|Delphi]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Amos|first=Trevor|date=2008|title=Pragmatic research design. An illustration of the use of the Delphi technique|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228359110|journal=Electronic Journal of Business Research Methods|volume=6|issue=2|pages=95–102}}</ref> and [[crowdsourcing]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eklund|first1=Lina|last2=Stamm|first2=Isabell|last3=Liebermann|first3=Wanda Katja|date=2019-10-01|title=The crowd in crowdsourcing: Crowdsourcing as a pragmatic research method|url=https://journals.uic.edu/ojs/index.php/fm/article/view/9206|journal=First Monday|volume=4|issue=10|language=en|doi=10.5210/fm.v24i10.9206|s2cid=204699798 |issn=1396-0466 |doi-access=free }}</ref> in fields such as urban planning.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=te Brömmelstroet|first=Marco|date=2017-10-01|title=Towards a pragmatic research agenda for the PSS domain|journal=Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice|language=en|volume=104|pages=77–83|doi=10.1016/j.tra.2016.05.011|s2cid=156431540 |issn=0965-8564|url=https://dare.uva.nl/personal/pure/en/publications/towards-a-pragmatic-research-agenda-for-the-pss-domain(b32b7fb8-e701-44dd-932a-d851dc32ce25).html |hdl=11245.1/b32b7fb8-e701-44dd-932a-d851dc32ce25|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

extract: A pragmatic clinical trial (PCT), sometimes called a practical clinical trial (PCT), is a clinical trial that focuses on correlation between treatments and outcomes in real-world health system practice rather than focusing on proving causative explanations for outcomes, which requires extensive deconfounding with inclusion and exclusion criteria so strict that they risk rendering the trial results irrelevant to much of real-world practice.
